title: Challenge 04: Branch Out
description: Creating a safe working branch and understanding why branches protect main.
concepts: Creating a safe working branch and understanding why branches protect main.
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're connecting three ideas that really belong together: your personal Learning Room repository, the branch you create for your own work, and the pull request workflow that turns a private edit into a real contribution.

[JAMIE]
So this is the moment where GitHub starts feeling less like a website full of tabs and more like an actual working environment.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And for this workshop, that environment is your Learning Room. It is your own private practice repository, created for you by GitHub Classroom. When you accepted the class assignment, GitHub copied a template repository into the workshop organization and made a personal repo for you, usually named something like learning-room-your-username.

[JAMIE]
Private is important there, right?

[ALEX]
Very. You are not editing the template repository itself. You are not changing organization permissions. You are not building your own GitHub organization. Facilitators handle all of that. Your job is to work inside your own copy. You have write access there, your own branches, your own pull requests, and your own automated feedback from the workshop bot.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Why go through all that instead of putting everyone into one shared repo from the start?

[ALEX]
Three reasons: safety, authenticity, and pace. Safety means you can experiment and recover without affecting anyone else. Authenticity means you still practice the real workflow: issues, branches, pull requests, checks, reviews, and merges. And pace means nobody is blocked by you, and you are not blocked by anyone else while you learn.

[JAMIE]
So it's protected practice, but still real GitHub.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. Day 2 moves you into more public collaboration spaces, but Day 1 builds the muscle memory in a controlled environment.

[JAMIE]
Can we walk through how someone actually gets into that repo in the first place?

[ALEX]
Yes. First, you open the GitHub Classroom assignment link in a browser where you're already signed into GitHub. Sometimes GitHub Classroom asks for authorization the first time. If so, you activate the authorize button. Then you may get a roster page where you identify yourself. If your name is missing, there's usually a skip link, and you tell a facilitator afterward.

[JAMIE]
Then comes the acceptance step.

[ALEX]
Right. Activate the button to accept the assignment. GitHub Classroom then starts copying the learning-room template into the workshop organization. The page may say something like you're ready to go, but it won't necessarily announce automatically when the repo link appears.

[JAMIE]
That sounds like one of those accessibility details people need to know ahead of time.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. With a screen reader, it helps to refresh every so often and move through links until you find your repository link. Once it appears, open it and verify a few things: the repository name matches your username, it looks like a private workshop copy, and you see the expected folders and files such as docs, .github, and README.

[JAMIE]
And bookmark it.

[ALEX]
Yes. That one step saves a surprising amount of friction.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What should be waiting for learners once the repo exists?

[ALEX]
Usually their first challenge issue. In the Issues tab, they should find a challenge created by automation. If it does not appear after a couple of minutes, they can refresh once, then check the Actions tab for the student progression workflow. If that workflow failed or never ran, they should contact a facilitator with the repo link.

[JAMIE]
And there's another bot we're supposed to notice early on too.

[ALEX]
Yes, Gandalf, the PR validation bot. Before you even open a pull request, you can visit the Actions tab and confirm there is a PR validation workflow present. You do not need to run it manually. You're just confirming the automation exists so later feedback won't feel mysterious.

[JAMIE]
So even before any coding or writing, learners are building a map: repo, issues, actions, automation.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And the readiness checkpoint is simple. Before moving on, you should be able to find docs slash CHALLENGES dot md, explain the flow issue to branch to pull request to review to merge, and know that Gandalf feedback appears in the pull request conversation.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
The chapter also talks about two learning tracks happening at once.

[ALEX]
It does. One track is optional GitHub Skills modules in your own account. Those are guided by GitHub's learning bot and give you extra self-paced practice. The other track is required: your Learning Room repository. That's the workshop path where you complete the actual Day 1 challenges.

[JAMIE]
So same account, different purposes.

[ALEX]
Yes. The Skills modules are optional skill drills. The Learning Room is the required workshop progression. They reinforce each other, but they are not the same thing.

[JAMIE]
And there are also those learning cards and tool cards sprinkled through the material.

[ALEX]
Right. Think of them as quick reference pieces. Some compare the two tracks. Some explain your practice branch. Some give tool-specific ways to switch branches or open pull requests. Even if we don't read them like flashcards here, their content matters.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's talk about the actual content inside the repo. What are learners working on?

[ALEX]
The Learning Room has a clear folder structure and several practice files. You'll work in files like docs slash welcome dot md, docs slash keyboard-shortcuts dot md, docs slash setup-guide dot md, and docs slash CHALLENGES dot md.

[JAMIE]
What kinds of tasks show up in those?

[ALEX]
In welcome dot md, there are intentional TODO sections. For example, learners may need to add content to parts like who can contribute, finding something to work on, or what happens after your contribution is merged. In keyboard-shortcuts dot md, there are screen reader shortcut references and intentional errors to fix. In setup-guide dot md, there may be broken links or incomplete steps. CHALLENGES dot md acts like the challenge menu.

[JAMIE]
And there are bonus challenges too.

[ALEX]
Yes. So the repo is not random. It is designed to give you authentic practice edits in accessible documentation contexts.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now we hit the phrase that matters for this challenge set: your practice branch.

[ALEX]
Exactly. A separate branch is where you make changes without affecting main. That isolation is the core concept. A branch lets you experiment, edit, revise, and even make mistakes without directly changing the main line of the repository.

[JAMIE]
So when beginners hear branch, they should not think advanced magic. They should think safe workspace.

[ALEX]
Beautifully put. Safe workspace. In the Learning Room chapter, the practice branch is your own ongoing branch for personal work. The reason for creating it is to separate your in-progress work from main. The way you use it is straightforward: switch to that branch before you start your edits, keep your work there, and later open pull requests from branch to main when a challenge asks you to.

[JAMIE]
And the tool cards would show how to switch to it depending on whether you're on the web, in Git, in VS Code, or elsewhere.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's zoom in on the specific challenge: Branch Out.

[ALEX]
This challenge asks you to create your personal branch for Day 1 work. The required naming pattern in the challenge issue is learn slash your GitHub username. So if your username is octocat, the branch would be learn slash octocat.

[JAMIE]
That sounds more specific than the general branch naming examples.

[ALEX]
Good catch. In general Git practice, many branch names are valid. Common patterns include things like fix slash welcome-todo, feature slash add-schedule-link, or docs slash update-readme. Short and descriptive is usually the goal. Type slash description is common, but not required.

[JAMIE]
But for this workshop challenge, the convention matters because automation and facilitators are looking for that exact style.

[ALEX]
Yes. For Challenge 4, the naming convention is not just preference. It helps the workshop systems identify your work. So although the solution reference says any branch name demonstrates the idea of isolation, the challenge itself asks for learn slash username, and that's the branch learners should create.

[JAMIE]
What if they type it wrong?

[ALEX]
Create a new branch with the correct name. The old one usually will not cause trouble. If GitHub says the branch already exists, that probably means you already created it and you just need to switch to it and verify the name.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Can we walk through how to create that branch on GitHub dot com first?

[ALEX]
Yes. Go to the repository's Code tab. Find the branch dropdown. By default it often shows main. Screen reader users may hear it announced as a button labeled something like switch branches or tags. Activate it, type learn slash your username, and choose the option to create that branch from main.

[JAMIE]
So the branch exists immediately on GitHub once you do that.

[ALEX]
Correct. And after that, the same branch control can also switch you to it.

[JAMIE]
That seems like the lowest-friction path for many learners.

[ALEX]
It is. And it matches the actual challenge instructions.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What about in VS Code with Git?

[ALEX]
You can create a branch in the terminal with git checkout dash b and then the branch name. For example, git checkout dash b learn slash your username. In VS Code, you can also use the Source Control interface by activating the branch name in the lower status bar and selecting create new branch.

[JAMIE]
And that's useful for learners who cloned the repo locally.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[JAMIE]
How about GitHub Desktop?

[ALEX]
In GitHub Desktop, open the Current Branch dropdown, choose New Branch, enter the branch name, and confirm it is based on main.

[JAMIE]
And the CLI path?

[ALEX]
If the repository isn't cloned yet, you can clone it with GitHub CLI, move into the repo directory, and then use the same Git branch creation command. The important part is that GitHub CLI helps you get the repo locally, but the branch creation itself is still plain Git.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
So if the learner used any one of those tools successfully, they completed the branch creation idea.

[ALEX]
Yes. The learning objective is not allegiance to a specific interface. It's understanding that branches let you work in isolation without affecting main.

[JAMIE]
But there's a wrinkle coming, because later PR exercises recommend a different branch naming pattern.

[ALEX]
Right, and this is an important distinction. Your personal learn slash username branch is your Day 1 personal practice branch. But in the pull request chapter, when you do a small focused change for a specific issue, you are often encouraged not to reuse that branch. Instead, use a short-lived feature branch like fix slash yourname dash issue number.

[JAMIE]
Why not just keep piling everything onto the learn branch?

[ALEX]
Because smaller, task-specific branches teach cleaner pull requests. One branch, one focused change, one PR. That makes review easier, keeps scope small, and mirrors good collaboration practice.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's build the pull request concept from the ground up. What is a pull request?

[ALEX]
A pull request is a structured request to merge changes from one branch into another, usually from your feature branch into main. It's where your work becomes a contribution. It holds the description, discussion, status checks, review comments, and merge controls all in one place.

[JAMIE]
So it's not just "please copy my code over." It's a conversation and validation space.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And the chapter is very intentional about accessibility here. It frames pull request work as something you can navigate with keyboard and screen reader, whether you're reading discussion, reviewing diffs, or checking automation.

[JAMIE]
There's also a setup note about GitHub's improved Files Changed experience.

[ALEX]
Yes. The material recommends using the newer Files Changed experience because it has better landmark structure and diff navigation support. Depending on your account, it may already be enabled automatically, may appear in feature preview, or may no longer be listed because it has become standard.

[JAMIE]
And there's a Browse Mode versus Focus Mode reminder for NVDA.

[ALEX]
Correct. Use Browse Mode for reading conversations, headings, and diffs. Switch to Focus Mode when you need to type into fields like comments or search. Then switch back. That simple habit can reduce a lot of frustration.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before the detailed navigation, the chapter lays out the workshop pattern for PR work.

[ALEX]
Yes: small change, linked PR, green checks. The Chapter 6 challenge set is built around that. First, create one small branch change. Second, open a linked pull request. Third, pass required checks.

[JAMIE]
And there's a nice CLI principles list too.

[ALEX]
There is. Check your current branch before pushing. Keep PR scope small. Include issue linkage as plain text using Closes number. Validate check status after each push, for example with GitHub CLI. And prefer documented command options rather than guessing.

[JAMIE]
That's a strong lesson for accessibility too: predictability beats cleverness.

[ALEX]
Very much so.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Walk us through that first small-change challenge.

[ALEX]
You start from your assigned issue in your Learning Room. That issue tells you which practice file to edit and what to fix. You navigate to the file in the repository, open it, and choose Edit this file.

[JAMIE]
And the source gives screen reader-specific hints there.

[ALEX]
Yes. For button navigation, NVDA or JAWS users might use quick navigation to buttons. VoiceOver users might use the rotor to find buttons. The point is that the edit control is reachable without a mouse.

[JAMIE]
Then you make a very small, focused edit.

[ALEX]
Right. Replace a TODO section, correct a shortcut value, fix a broken link, complete an incomplete instruction. Only what the issue asked for. Then when you commit through the web editor, you enter a branch name, usually fix slash yourname dash issue number, select the option to create a new branch for this commit and start a pull request, and propose changes.

[JAMIE]
So GitHub can create the branch as part of the editing flow.

[ALEX]
Exactly, which makes it very beginner-friendly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Then comes opening the pull request itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. On the Open a pull request page, you fill in the title and body. The title should briefly describe the change. The body should explain what changed and why. And critically, it should include the issue-linking line: Closes number.

[JAMIE]
Why is that line such a big deal?

[ALEX]
Because when the PR is merged, GitHub can automatically close the linked issue. It also helps reviewers immediately understand what problem the PR is meant to solve.

[JAMIE]
And you also verify that the base branch is main and the compare branch is your feature branch.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Then create the pull request.

[JAMIE]
The materials also mention PR forms more broadly: title, description, summary, changes, related issues, testing, screenshots or recordings.

[ALEX]
Yes. Even in simple workshop PRs, those categories matter. A reviewer wants to know what changed, why, what issue it relates to, how you checked it, and whether any visual evidence matters. Not every field is equally relevant for every doc change, but the mindset is important.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
And draft pull requests show up here too.

[ALEX]
They do. A draft pull request is useful when you want feedback before the work is fully ready to merge. A draft is visible, but it signals "not ready for final review." Later, you can mark it ready for review. You can also convert an open PR back to draft if needed.

[JAMIE]
So draft changes the social meaning more than the basic container.

[ALEX]
Exactly. It's still a pull request, but with a different readiness signal.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Once a PR exists, learners need to know how to find and read it.

[ALEX]
Yes. You can reach pull requests from notifications, from the repository's Pull Requests tab, or with GitHub keyboard shortcuts. In browser workflows, shortcut sequences can help jump to issues or PRs. In terminal workflows, GitHub CLI can list open PRs, filter them, show a specific PR, or open one in the browser.

[JAMIE]
So there are both web and CLI routes for navigation, not just creation.

[ALEX]
Right. And once you're on the PR list page, you're looking at a queue of contributions. From there, you open an individual PR page.

[JAMIE]
Which has its own anatomy.

[ALEX]
Exactly. A pull request page includes a tab bar, typically with Conversation, Commits, Checks, and Files Changed. Learning that structure is huge, because it tells you where to go depending on your question.

[JAMIE]
For example, if I want the explanation and discussion, I use Conversation.

[ALEX]
Yes. If you want commit history, go to Commits. If you want CI or bot results, go to Checks. If you want the actual diff, go to Files Changed.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's slow down on the Conversation tab, because that's where a lot of learners first meet review as a lived thing.

[ALEX]
The Conversation tab usually contains the PR description, the status checks summary, and any comments or reviews. You read the description to understand scope. You read the checks section to see whether validation passed or failed. And you read the review comments to understand questions, concerns, or requested changes.

[JAMIE]
Including conversations that might later be resolved.

[ALEX]
Yes. Resolving a conversation usually means the underlying issue has been addressed and the thread no longer needs to stay open. That can reduce clutter, but it should only be done when the concern has truly been handled.

[JAMIE]
In this workshop, Gandalf's feedback appears in Conversation too.

[ALEX]
Correct. And there are three broad types of feedback in the Learning Room system. Automated bot feedback arrives quickly, often around 30 seconds. Peer reviewer feedback may take longer, perhaps 15 to 60 minutes. And merge-time automation tracks your progress and can unlock the next challenge.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What about the Commits tab?

[ALEX]
The Commits tab shows the individual commits included in the pull request. That can help you understand the sequence of work, especially if the PR changed over time in response to feedback.

[JAMIE]
And the Checks tab?

[ALEX]
That's where status checks and workflow results live in more detail. If a check fails, the Checks tab often gives deeper logs or summaries than the short status snippet in Conversation. In the workshop context, this is especially useful when Gandalf or another validation workflow reports a problem.

[JAMIE]
So if the bot says something failed, you don't just panic. You go investigate.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now the Files Changed tab. This is where many screen reader users have historically had a rougher time.

[ALEX]
Yes, and the chapter addresses that directly. The newer interface includes a file tree panel and more navigable diffs. In Files Changed, you can move through changed files, enter a file's diff, and read line-by-line changes.

[JAMIE]
How are those lines typically interpreted?

[ALEX]
A plus line means added content. A minus line means removed content. Context lines show surrounding unchanged text. So when a learner hears a diff, they are not hearing a finished document; they are hearing a record of change.

[JAMIE]
That distinction matters a lot.

[ALEX]
It does. Especially in docs work, where a diff might contain only a few inserted lines in the middle of a paragraph or heading structure.

[JAMIE]
And inline comments can be placed on diff lines too.

[ALEX]
Yes. You can place comments on a specific line, or even create multi-line comments. The chapter notes that the exact interaction details differ between Windows and macOS, but conceptually you select the location in the diff, open the comment control, type the feedback, and submit it as part of a review or as a standalone comment.

[JAMIE]
And existing comments can also appear inside the diff.

[ALEX]
Right. Which is helpful because it keeps feedback anchored to the code or text being discussed.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's come back to the workshop challenge where checks have to pass. What is the learner looking for from Gandalf?

[ALEX]
After opening the PR, wait a short while and then read the validation comment. Gandalf checks things like whether the PR references an issue using Closes number, whether the description has enough detail, whether the changed files are in the expected place, and accessibility-oriented content checks such as heading hierarchy, descriptive link text, and valid alt text.

[JAMIE]
So the bot is not just being fussy. It is teaching contribution quality.

[ALEX]
Exactly. If feedback is given, you update the branch, push or commit again, and the checks rerun. This repeat cycle is normal. It is not a sign of failure. It is the pull request loop doing its job.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
The learning room chapter also explains PR sharing. Can you map that out?

[ALEX]
Yes. First, the student opens a pull request. Then automation validates it. Then, if peer review is part of the activity, a facilitator may arrange reviewer access or pairings. The reviewer reads and comments. The author responds and updates. Finally, the PR is merged and the progression bot may post the next challenge.

[JAMIE]
And visibility is mentioned repeatedly.

[ALEX]
Right. Because in a private per-student repo, visibility is intentionally limited. You generally do not see everyone else's work by default. Peer review access may be granted when needed. That balance protects privacy while still allowing realistic collaboration.

[JAMIE]
So when the FAQ asks can I see other students' PRs, the answer is basically not automatically.

[ALEX]
Correct. And related FAQ answers matter too. If you disagree with a reviewer, respond respectfully and seek facilitator help if needed. If your PR seems buried, it generally is not lost just because many others are working at once. If your reviewer doesn't respond, ask for help. If bot feedback seems wrong, investigate and escalate rather than silently ignoring it. And no, you do not necessarily need to complete every possible challenge to learn something meaningful, though the workshop will have required paths.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There's also practical advice on reviewing a peer's PR.

[ALEX]
Yes. Find the PR you're assigned to. Read it carefully. Look at the description before judging the diff. Leave a review with clear, respectful feedback. And if you're the author receiving feedback, respond constructively rather than defensively.

[JAMIE]
That's a professional skill, not just a GitHub skill.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. The tooling is only half the lesson.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Can we talk about submitting a review? What options do reviewers actually have?

[ALEX]
A reviewer can start a review by adding comments on files, then complete and submit it. The final review verdict is often one of three things: approve, request changes, or comment without a formal verdict. In command-line workflows, GitHub CLI can also help view diffs and submit review outcomes.

[JAMIE]
And there are GitHub keyboard shortcuts for PR work too.

[ALEX]
Yes, including shortcuts on the PR list page, on an open PR, and inside Files Changed. Learners do not need to memorize every key immediately, but knowing these shortcuts exist can make review much faster and more accessible.

[JAMIE]
What about suggested changes?

[ALEX]
Those are especially useful in review. A reviewer can propose exact replacement text directly in the review. Then the author can apply the suggestion, often with a click, which turns the feedback into a commit. Multiple suggestions can sometimes be batched into one commit. Suggestions are best when you know the specific fix. Plain comments are better when you want to explain a concern without prescribing exact wording.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
And then eventually someone merges.

[ALEX]
Yes. Maintainers may see different merge options. A standard merge commit preserves branch history. Squash and merge combines the branch's commits into one. Rebase and merge applies the changes without a merge commit. There may also be options to delete the branch after merging and to enable auto-merge so the PR merges automatically once required checks pass.

[JAMIE]
That's good to know even if learners are not repository maintainers everywhere.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Understanding the options helps you interpret what happened to your contribution after approval.

[JAMIE]
And after a PR is merged?

[ALEX]
The linked issue may close automatically. The branch may be deleted. In the Learning Room, merge-time automation may also record progress and unlock the next challenge.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Auto-merge sounds worth a quick explanation too.

[ALEX]
Auto-merge is useful when approval is done but checks are still running. You enable it on the PR, choose the merge method if allowed, and GitHub completes the merge automatically when the requirements are satisfied. You can also cancel auto-merge if circumstances change.

[JAMIE]
So it's a convenience feature, not a different review philosophy.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
The chapter also offers practical scenarios. Can we make those concrete?

[ALEX]
Scenario one: you want to review an assigned PR. You find the PR, read the description, inspect the diff, check the bot results, and then leave review feedback. Scenario two: you want to respond to review feedback on your own PR. You read comments carefully, update your branch, reply where helpful, and re-check status. Scenario three: your PR has a merge conflict. That means your branch and the base branch have incompatible changes that need to be reconciled before merge.

[JAMIE]
That last one often scares beginners.

[ALEX]
Yes, but it's a workflow problem, not a moral failing.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What mistakes should learners try to avoid when opening PRs?

[ALEX]
Common mistakes include making the PR too large, forgetting to link the issue, leaving the description vague, ignoring failing checks, and mixing unrelated changes into one branch. Reviewers look for clarity, scope control, and enough context to trust what they're reading.

[JAMIE]
So a good PR description really matters.

[ALEX]
It does. The chapter emphasizes writing descriptions that get reviewed. That means a useful summary, a clear list of changes made, related issues, testing notes, and a checklist when appropriate. The Closes number pattern is especially important. Before-and-after framing can also help reviewers understand the impact.

[JAMIE]
And there's even a template idea.

[ALEX]
Yes. Essentially: what changed, why it changed, which issue it closes, how it was tested, and anything else the reviewer should notice. The source even contrasts good and bad descriptions, because "fixed stuff" is not enough.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
I also noticed the chapter includes a try-it exercise where you read a real pull request.

[ALEX]
That's a great learning move. Open a PR, read the description, inspect the conversation, and then visit Files Changed to connect the written explanation to the actual diff. For a blind or low-vision learner, this is how the interface stops being abstract. You learn where things are by traversing them in order.

[JAMIE]
And there's a broader message there too: manual review comes before any AI-assisted review.

[ALEX]
Yes. The material is very clear that assistive or agentic review tools can help summarize diffs or draft comments, but they do not replace your judgment. You need to know how to read a pull request yourself before delegating any part of the review process.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we wrap, I want to return to the specific evidence the Branch Out challenge asks for.

[ALEX]
Good idea. The challenge asks learners to confirm their branch name and describe how they created it. So a complete response might say, "My branch name is learn slash myusername. I created it from the branch dropdown on the Code tab," or describe doing it in VS Code, GitHub Desktop, or the command line.

[JAMIE]
And there's also a peer simulation note.

[ALEX]
Yes. Learners are encouraged to open the peer-simulation PR and notice its branch name. And if they have a real buddy nearby, they can check whether that person created their branch and help them find the branch dropdown if they are stuck.

[JAMIE]
Which reinforces that branch names are visible collaboration signals, not just private labels.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's end with the big picture. What matters most here?

[ALEX]
Your Learning Room is your private practice space. Branches give you safe isolation. Pull requests turn branch work into reviewed, validated, mergeable contributions. The workshop uses bots, issue linkage, and accessibility-aware feedback not to slow you down, but to teach you the habits of real open source work.

[JAMIE]
And in the short term, for this challenge, the win is simple: create your personal branch, usually named learn slash your username, and understand why it exists.

[ALEX]
Yes. Then when later exercises ask for a smaller task-specific branch and a pull request, you'll know that the branch is not just a hoop to jump through. It is the container that makes review, automation, and collaboration possible.

[JAMIE]
So the flow becomes intuitive: issue, branch, pull request, review, merge.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And once that sequence feels familiar, contributing becomes much less intimidating.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
One final note: when you need the current source of truth, use official GitHub documentation, the GitHub changelog, and GitHub's accessibility guidance for pull requests and CLI workflows. Workshop material teaches the workflow, but official docs remain authoritative as interfaces evolve.

[JAMIE]
That's a good habit for any tech learner.

[ALEX]
It is. And with that, you're ready to branch out, open pull requests with purpose, and start contributing with confidence.

name: "Challenge 4: Branch Out"
description: Create your personal branch for Day 1 work.
hidden: true
title: "Challenge 4: Branch Out (@{username})"
labels: ["challenge", "day-1"]
body:
  - type: markdown
    attributes:
      value: |
        ## Challenge 4: Branch Out

        **Chapter:** [Ch06: Working with Pull Requests](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/06-working-with-pull-requests.md)

        **What you will do:** Create a personal branch named `learn/YOUR-USERNAME` where you will make your Day 1 changes.

        ### Instructions

        1. Make sure you are on the **Code** tab of the learning-room repository.
        2. Find the branch dropdown (it shows "main" by default).
        3. Type `learn/YOUR-USERNAME` (replace YOUR-USERNAME with your actual GitHub username).
        4. Select **Create branch: learn/YOUR-USERNAME from main**.

        ### Branch naming convention

        Your branch name must follow this pattern: `learn/` followed by your GitHub username. Examples:

        - `learn/octocat`
        - `learn/mona-lisa`
        - `learn/student42`

        This naming convention helps facilitators and automation identify your work.

  - type: textarea
    id: evidence
    attributes:
      label: "Your evidence"
      description: "Confirm your branch name and describe how you created it."
      placeholder: |
        My branch name: learn/myusername
        I created it by...
    validations:
      required: true

  - type: markdown
    attributes:
      value: |
        ### Peer simulation check

        Open the peer-simulation PR and notice its branch name. If you have a real buddy, ask whether they created their branch and help them find the branch dropdown if they are stuck.

        ### If you get stuck

        | Symptom | Try this |
        |---|---|
        | I cannot find the branch dropdown | Look for a button that says "main" with a dropdown arrow, near the top-left of the file list. Screen reader users: it is a button labeled "Switch branches/tags". |
        | It says the branch already exists | If you already created it, you are done. Switch to it and confirm your username is in the name. |
        | I typed the name wrong | Create a new branch with the correct name. The old one will not cause problems. |
        | I finished but want to check my work | [View the reference solution](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/solutions/solution-04-branch-out.md) |

# Solution Reference: Challenge 4 -- Branch Out

This shows how to create a branch from each tool. You only needed to use one.

## On github.com

1. Go to the repository's Code tab
2. Click the branch dropdown (it says "main")
3. Type a new branch name like `fix/welcome-todo`
4. Click "Create branch: fix/welcome-todo from main"

The branch now exists on GitHub. You can switch to it using the same dropdown.

## In VS Code (with Git)

```
git checkout -b fix/welcome-todo
```

Or use the Source Control sidebar: click the branch name in the bottom-left status bar, then select "Create new branch."

## In GitHub Desktop

1. Click the Current Branch dropdown
2. Click "New Branch"
3. Enter the name `fix/welcome-todo`
4. Confirm it is based on `main`

## With GitHub CLI

```
gh repo clone <workshop-org>/learning-room-<your-username>
cd learning-room
git checkout -b fix/welcome-todo
```

## Branch naming

Good branch names are short and descriptive:

- `fix/welcome-todo` -- fixing a TODO in welcome.md
- `feature/add-schedule-link` -- adding a new link
- `docs/update-readme` -- documentation change

All of these are valid. The convention `type/description` is common but not required.

## What matters

The learning objective is understanding that branches let you work in isolation without affecting main. If you created any branch with any name, you completed this challenge.

# The Learning Room: Your Personal Practice Repository
>
> **Listen to Episode 4:** [The Learning Room](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix A: Glossary](appendix-a-glossary.md) | [Appendix C: Markdown Reference](appendix-c-markdown-reference.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [GitHub Docs: About README files](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-readmes) | [GitHub Docs: Editing files](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-files/editing-files)

## What Is the Learning Room?

The **Learning Room** is your **own private GitHub repository** for the workshop. When you accept the GitHub Classroom assignment in Block 0, GitHub copies the [`Community-Access/learning-room-template`](https://github.com/Community-Access/learning-room-template) repository into the workshop classroom organization as `<workshop-org>/learning-room-<your-username>`. That copy is yours to use for the workshop - you have write access, your own branches, your own pull requests, and your own automated feedback from Gandalf the PR validation bot.

You do **not** work directly in `Community-Access/learning-room-template`. Think of the template as the clean master copy facilitators maintain. Your work happens in the private Learning Room repository created for you by GitHub Classroom.

Throughout this chapter and the rest of Day 1, "your Learning Room repository" or "your Learning Room repo" refers to this private copy. Every student gets one, and every copy starts from the same template files. You will not see other students' work in your repo, and they will not see yours - but everyone is doing the same challenges in parallel. Peer-simulation issues and pull requests inside your repo provide realistic collaboration practice, and facilitators may also pair students for real peer review when access is intentionally provided.

You do **not** need to create a GitHub organization or change repository permission settings. The workshop organization, template repository, Classroom assignment, and GitHub Actions permissions are managed by the facilitators.

## Why a Per-Student Repo?

GitHub Classroom gives each participant their own repository for three reasons:

- **Safety** -- you can experiment, break things, and recover without affecting anyone else
- **Authenticity** -- you practice real repository work: issues, branches, pull requests, checks, reviews, and merging
- **Pace** -- you progress through the 9 Day 1 challenges as fast or as slow as you need; nobody is waiting on you and you are not blocking anybody else

Real open source projects are shared spaces, and you will absolutely contribute to one on Day 2 (`accessibility-agents`) and through the Bonus C challenge. The Learning Room exists so you can build the muscle memory for issue, branch, PR, review, merge in a space where every mistake is a learning opportunity, not a public problem.

## Step-by-Step: Accept Your Classroom Assignment and Open Your Repo

This is the very first hands-on step of Day 1. By the end of this walkthrough you will have your own Learning Room repository on GitHub and your first challenge issue waiting for you. The whole flow takes about five minutes.

> **What you need before you start:**
>
> - A GitHub account you are signed into in your browser ([Pre-Workshop Setup, Step 1](00-pre-workshop-setup.md#step-1---create-your-github-account))
> - The **Classroom assignment link** -- the facilitator pastes this link in the workshop chat at the start of Block 0. It looks like `https://classroom.github.com/a/<random-id>`. If you do not have it, ask in chat or DM the facilitator.

### 1. Open the assignment link

1. In the same browser where you are signed into GitHub, open the Classroom assignment link the facilitator shared.
2. The page that loads is hosted on `classroom.github.com`. Your screen reader announces a heading with the assignment name (for example, "Git Going with GitHub").
3. If the page asks you to authorize **GitHub Classroom** to access your GitHub account, activate **Authorize GitHub Classroom**. This is a one-time step.

### 2. Identify yourself (if asked)

GitHub Classroom may ask you to pick your name from a roster so the facilitators can match your GitHub username to the registration list.

1. If a roster page appears, navigate the list with arrow keys or use Find-in-Page (`Ctrl+F` / `Cmd+F`) to search for your name.
2. Activate the link or button next to your name.
3. If you do not see your name on the roster, activate the **Skip to the next step** link and tell the facilitator in chat. They will reconcile the roster after your repo is created.

### 3. Accept the assignment

1. You now see a screen with a button that says **Accept this assignment** (or just **Accept the assignment**). Activate it.
2. The page changes to a status screen that says something like "You are ready to go!" with a refresh option. GitHub Classroom is now copying the `learning-room-template` repository into the workshop classroom organization and granting you access to your private copy. This usually takes 10-30 seconds.
3. Activate the **Refresh** link (or reload the page with `F5`) every 15 seconds or so until you see a link to your new repository. The link looks like `https://github.com/<workshop-org>/learning-room-<your-username>`.

> **Screen reader tip:** The status page does not auto-announce when the repo is ready. Use Browse mode and press `K` to step through links until you hear your repository link, or refresh the page until it appears.

### 4. Open your new repository

1. Activate the link to your repository. You land on the standard GitHub repo page for `<workshop-org>/learning-room-<your-username>`.
2. Verify three things on this page:
   - The **repo name** in the heading matches `learning-room-<your-username>`.
   - The **About** sidebar (or repo description) confirms this is a private workshop copy.
   - You see folders like `docs/`, `.github/`, and files like `README.md`. These came from the template.
3. Bookmark this page. You will return here for every Day 1 challenge.

### 5. Find your first challenge issue

When your Learning Room repo is ready, **Challenge 1** appears as a GitHub issue in your repo. The facilitators prepare this by running the Student Progression Bot after students accept the Classroom assignment. The next challenges unlock one at a time as you close the previous ones.

1. From your repository page, navigate to the **Issues** tab. Keyboard shortcut: press `G` then `I`.
2. You should see at least one open issue with a title like **"Challenge 1: Find Your Way Around"** authored by `aria-bot` (or `github-actions[bot]`).
3. Open Challenge 1. Read the issue body -- it tells you what to do, where to find evidence, and how to submit completion.

> **If Challenge 1 is missing after 2 minutes:** Refresh the Issues tab once. If it still does not appear:
>
> 1. Open the **Actions** tab and check whether the **Student Progression Bot** workflow ran successfully.
> 2. If it failed or never ran, post a message in the workshop chat with the link to your repo. The facilitator can trigger `student-progression.yml` or create Challenge 1 from the issue template.

### 6. Confirm Gandalf can talk to you

The PR validation bot, **Gandalf**, posts educational feedback whenever you open a pull request. To confirm Gandalf is wired up, open the **Actions** tab in your repo and look for a workflow named **pr-validation-bot** (or **Gandalf PR Validation**). The workflow should appear in the list even before you have opened a PR. You do not need to run anything yet -- you just want to confirm it exists.

You are now done with Block 0. Continue with the chapter below to learn how the Learning Room is organized, then jump to [Chapter 5](05-working-with-issues.md) to start Challenge 1.

## Workshop Recommendation (Chapter 4)

Chapter 4 is a **system orientation chapter**.

- **Challenge count:** none
- **Automation check:** none
- **Why:** this chapter explains how your repo is set up and prepares you for the issue-based challenges that start in Chapter 5.

### Readiness Checkpoint

Before starting Chapter 5 challenges, you should be able to:

1. Find `docs/CHALLENGES.md` in your Learning Room repository.
2. Explain the flow: issue -> branch -> pull request -> review -> merge.
3. Identify where Gandalf bot feedback appears on a PR (the Conversation tab).

## Two Tracks That Reinforce Each Other

Throughout Day 1 you work on **two parallel learning tracks**, both in your own account:

### Track 1: GitHub Skills Modules (Optional Self-Paced Practice)

- **[Introduction to GitHub](https://github.com/skills/introduction-to-github)** - Create branch, open PR, merge
- **[Communicate Using Markdown](https://github.com/skills/communicate-using-markdown)** - Write headings, links, code, tables
- **[Review Pull Requests](https://github.com/skills/review-pull-requests)** - Comment, approve, suggest changes

**Scope:** Your personal account, optional and self-paced
**Bot:** Mona (GitHub's automated learning bot) guides each step
**Purpose:** Hands-on practice of individual skills, complementary to the workshop

### Track 2: Your Learning Room Repository (Required Workshop Track)

- **Blocks 1-4 (Day 1 morning/afternoon):** Challenges 1-7 -- find your way, file an issue, branch, commit, open a PR, survive a merge conflict
- **Block 5 (Day 1 evening):** Challenges 8-9 -- culture and merge day
- **Block 6 (Day 1 evening):** Community tools (labels, milestones, notifications)

**Scope:** Your private Learning Room repository (created from `learning-room-template` via Classroom)
**Bot:** **Gandalf** -- a PR validation bot that posts educational feedback on every push, plus a Student Progression bot that auto-creates the next challenge issue when you close the current one
**Purpose:** End-to-end practice of the full workflow in a real repository where you have full control

#### How the Two Tracks Compare

| Step | GitHub Skills (optional) | Your Learning Room (required) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Create a branch in a Skills repo | Create a branch in your Learning Room |
| 2 | Open a PR | Open a PR |
| 3 | Get instant bot feedback from Mona | Get instant bot feedback from Gandalf |
| 4 | Mona verifies your step | Gandalf validates structure; you self-merge or peer-review |
| 5 | Next Skills step unlocked | Closing the issue auto-unlocks the next challenge |

### Learning Cards: Two Tracks, One Account

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- GitHub Skills modules run in your personal account; press `G I` from any Skills repo to see the issue thread where Mona posts instructions
- Your Learning Room repository lives at a different URL inside the workshop organization; bookmark it and use `Alt+D` (address bar) to confirm which repo you are in
- Gandalf's bot comments on your PRs appear as PR conversation comments; press `3` on the PR page to jump between them

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- GitHub Skills repos have a distinct green banner at the top of the README that says "Start course"; your Learning Room repo has no such banner
- Check the repository name in the top-left header to confirm which track you are working in (Skills repo vs. your Learning Room)
- Gandalf's avatar appears next to bot comments; your human reviewer's avatar appears next to peer review comments

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- Skills modules appear as separate repos under your account page (github.com/your-username); your Learning Room appears under the workshop organization assigned by your facilitators
- Gandalf's comments have a distinct grey bot badge next to the username, just like Mona's
- Keep both repos open in separate browser tabs so you can switch between tracks during the workshop

</details>

## Your Learning Room Folder Structure

Every Learning Room repository (yours and every other participant's) starts as an exact copy of `learning-room-template` and contains these files and folders:

- **README.md** -- Getting started guide
- **.github/**
  - **STUDENT_GUIDE.md** -- How the bot works
  - **IMPLEMENTATION_GUIDE.md** -- Full setup walkthrough
  - **SETUP_AND_MAINTENANCE.md** -- Maintenance reference
  - **workflows/** -- 3 automation workflows
    - learning-room-pr-bot.yml (PR validation)
    - student-progression.yml (challenge delivery)
    - skills-progression.yml (achievement tracking)
    - student-grouping.yml (peer pairing)
  - **scripts/**
    - validate-pr.js (validation logic)
  - **data/**
    - student-roster.json (your cohort info)
    - challenge-progression.json (levels, badges)
- **docs/**
  - CHALLENGES.md -- 21 challenges (16 core + 5 bonus)
  - welcome.md -- Has a TODO to complete
  - keyboard-shortcuts.md -- Has intentional errors
  - setup-guide.md -- Has broken links
- Other files for practice

## Your Practice Branch

In your own Learning Room repository, **you decide what branches to create**. The Day 1 challenge sequence asks you to work on a single feature branch named after yourself:

> **Branch naming convention for Day 1:** `learn/<your-github-username>` (all lowercase)

**Examples:**

- If your GitHub username is `payown`, your branch is `learn/payown`
- If your username is `BudgieMom`, your branch is `learn/budgiemom`
- If your username is `Weijun-Zhang-1996`, your branch is `learn/weijun-zhang-1996`

### Why you create a separate branch

- **Protected main branch** - The `main` branch in your Learning Room is protected; changes have to land via pull request even though you own the repo. This mirrors how mature open source projects work.
- **Your workspace** - Your `learn/<username>` branch is where you commit and push changes before opening a PR
- **Clean history** - Keeping experiments off `main` until they are reviewed (by you, by Gandalf, or by a peer) keeps your project history easy to read
- **Realistic workflow** - Contributors to real open source projects always create feature branches before opening a PR. You are practicing exactly that pattern.

### How to use your branch

The Day 1 challenges (4 onward) walk you through creating and using your branch on GitHub.com. Once you start working locally in Chapter 14, the same branch is what you check out:

```bash
git checkout learn/<your-github-username>
```

1. Create the branch on GitHub.com (Challenge 4) or locally with `git checkout -b learn/<username>` from `main`
2. Make your changes and commit them to the branch
3. Push the branch to GitHub if you created it locally
4. Open a pull request from `learn/<username>` -> `main` (Challenge 6)

> **Which branch do I use and when?**
>
> | Chapter | Branch needed? | What to use |
> |---------|---------------|-------------|
> | Chapter 5 (Issues) | No | Work happens in issue threads directly. No branch or file editing required. |
> | Chapter 6 (PRs, web editor) | Yes | Create `learn/<username>` from `main` (Challenge 4) and edit on it. |
> | Chapter 6 (PRs, local clone) | Yes, create manually | `git checkout -b learn/<username>` from `main`. |
> | Chapter 14+ (Local Git) | Yes | Reuse `learn/<username>`, or create additional `fix/<short-description>` branches from `main` for new work. |
>
> **Summary:** Chapter 5 needs no branch. Chapters 6-7 use the same `learn/<username>` branch. Day 2 reuses that branch and adds short-lived `fix/` branches when you tackle additional issues.

### Learning Cards: Your Practice Branch

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- To switch branches on GitHub.com, press `W` (in Focus Mode) to open the branch selector, type your branch name (`learn/<username>`), and press `Enter` when it appears
- In VS Code's terminal, type `git checkout learn/<your-github-username>` (lowercase)
- Press `Ctrl+Shift+G` in VS Code to open Source Control; the current branch name is announced at the top of the panel

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- The branch selector button shows the current branch name (e.g., "main") above the file table; click it and type "learn" to filter to your branch
- After switching branches, the branch name updates in the selector button; verify it reads `learn/<username>`, not "main"
- In VS Code, the current branch name appears in the bottom-left corner of the Status Bar in small text; zoom in or check Source Control panel header for a larger display

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The branch selector is the dropdown button above the file table showing the current branch name with a down-arrow icon
- Your branch follows the pattern `learn/<username>` (all lowercase); type "learn" in the dropdown search to find it quickly
- In VS Code, the current branch is shown in the bottom-left of the Status Bar; click it to switch branches via a dropdown

</details>

### Tool Cards: Switch to Your Practice Branch

**github.com (browser):**

1. On the repository page, click the branch selector dropdown (shows "main").
2. Type `learn` to filter, then select `learn/<username>`.

**github.dev (web editor):**

1. Click the branch name in the bottom-left status bar.
2. Select your `learn/<username>` branch from the list.

**VS Code Desktop:**

1. Click the branch name in the bottom-left status bar (or press `Ctrl+Shift+P` then type **Git: Checkout to**).
2. Select `origin/learn/<username>` from the branch list.

**GitHub Desktop:**

1. Click the **Current Branch** dropdown at the top.
2. Type `learn` to filter, then select `learn/<username>`.

**Git CLI (terminal):**

```bash
git checkout learn/<username>
```

---

## The Practice Files: What You Will Work On

> **See also:** [Appendix C: Markdown Reference](appendix-c-markdown-reference.md) covers all Markdown syntax with accessible examples -- you will need it for editing these files.

The `docs/` folder contains three practice files with intentional issues. These are the files you will edit, fix, and submit pull requests for during the contribution sprint. Here is exactly what you will encounter in each file.

### docs/welcome.md - Introduction to Open Source Contribution

This file introduces newcomers to open source. It has **three [TODO] sections** where content is missing:

#### [TODO] 1 - "Who Can Contribute?" section
>
> [TODO: Add a paragraph explaining that contributors come from all backgrounds, skill levels, and countries. Emphasize that using assistive technology is not a barrier to contribution - in fact, AT users bring a perspective that improves projects for everyone.]

#### [TODO] 2 - "Finding Something to Work On" section
>
> [TODO: Add two or three sentences about how to read an issue to decide if it is right for you. What questions should you ask yourself? Is the description clear enough? Is anyone else already working on it?]

#### [TODO] 3 - "After Your Contribution Is Merged" section
>
> [TODO: Add a sentence or two about what this means for someone's GitHub profile and open source portfolio.]

It also has a broken internal link that needs to be found and fixed. **Challenges 1 and 3** from CHALLENGES.md map directly to this file.

### docs/keyboard-shortcuts.md - Screen Reader Shortcut Reference

This is a comprehensive reference with tables for NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver shortcuts. It contains **intentional errors** in some shortcut references that students need to find and fix.

The file has three major sections:

- **NVDA (Windows)** - Single-key navigation, mode switching, reading commands
- **JAWS (Windows)** - Virtual cursor navigation, mode switching, reading commands
- **VoiceOver (macOS)** - Rotor navigation, VO commands for GitHub

Plus cross-platform shortcuts for GitHub pages and common workarounds.

**Challenge 2** asks you to add a missing shortcut to the correct table. When you edit this file, you must preserve the Markdown table formatting. The bot validates that tables remain well-formed.

### docs/setup-guide.md - Getting Ready to Contribute

This step-by-step guide walks through GitHub account setup, accessibility settings, screen reader configuration, and repository forking. It contains **broken links** that point to incorrect URLs and **incomplete steps**.

Look for:

- Links to GitHub settings pages that may have changed
- A `[TODO]` note at the bottom referencing items for facilitators
- Steps that reference forking a "workshop repository" without providing the actual URL

This file is used for **intermediate and advanced challenges** (Challenges 4-6) where students fix heading hierarchy, improve link text, and add missing descriptions.

### docs/CHALLENGES.md - Your Challenge Menu

This file lists all 21 challenges organized by progression level:

| Level | Challenges | Requirement |
| -------  | -----------  | -------------  |
| Explorer (01-03) | Scavenger hunt, first issue, join conversation | Getting started |
| Contributor (04-07) | Branch out, make your mark, first PR, merge conflict | 3+ challenges |
| Collaborator (08-09) | Culture reflection, merge day | 7+ challenges |
| Operator (10-11) | Go local, Day 2 PR | 9+ challenges |
| Reviewer (12-14) | Code review, Copilot, issue template | 11+ challenges |
| Agent Navigator (15-16) | Agents, capstone | 14+ challenges |
| Bonus (A-E) | Accessibility audit, mentor, cross-repo, workflow, docs | Optional |

Each challenge lists the file(s) to edit, estimated time, skills practiced, and success criteria.

### Bonus Challenges

Five bonus challenges (A through E) are available for students who finish faster. These include an accessibility audit, mentoring a peer, cross-repository contribution, creating a custom workflow, and documentation improvement.

## How PR Sharing Works

### Step 1: Student Opens a PR

#### Student A (working on Challenge 3: Complete Welcome Guide)

1. Finds their assigned issue (Issues tab → filter `Assignee:@me`)
2. Opens `docs/welcome.md` and edits the three `[TODO]` sections
3. Commits to a new branch: `fix/studentA-issue12`
4. Opens a pull request with description:

   ```markdown
   ## What Changed
   Completed the three [TODO] sections in docs/welcome.md:
   - Added contributor backgrounds paragraph
   - Added guidance on evaluating issues
   - Added note about GitHub profile impact

   Closes #12
   ```

5. **Submits the PR**

**Visibility:** The PR immediately appears in the repo's Pull Requests tab. All students can see it.

### Step 2: Automation Bot Validates

#### Bot (`.github/workflows/learning-room-pr-bot.yml`)

- Runs within 30 seconds
- Checks:
  - Issue reference (does PR link to issue with `Closes #12`?)
  - File location (only `docs/` directory files changed?)
  - Markdown accessibility (headings, links, alt text, broken links)
  - [TODO] markers (all three removed from welcome.md?)
- Posts a comprehensive comment with:
  - Required checks (must pass)
  - Suggestions (optional improvements)
  - Accessibility analysis (detailed issues + fixes)
  - Learning resources (links to docs)
- Applies labels (documentation, accessibility, needs-review)
- Creates commit status check visible in PR checks

**Visibility:** The bot comment appears in your PR. You see it; the facilitators see it; nobody else does unless they have been added as a collaborator on your repo.

### Step 3: Peer Review (Facilitator-Arranged)

The `learning-room-template` ships with a peer-pairing workflow (`.github/workflows/student-grouping.yml`) that was designed for a single shared repo. Under the GitHub Classroom model used in this workshop, **peer review is arranged by the facilitators rather than auto-assigned**, because each student's repo is private.

When Challenge 3 ("Join the Conversation") or Challenge 8 ("Culture") asks for peer review:

1. The facilitators (Jeff and Michael) pair you with another participant.
2. They add each of you as a collaborator on the other's Learning Room repo.
3. Each of you receives a notification: "You have been added as a collaborator."
4. You can now read the other person's PRs, leave comments, request changes, and approve.
5. After the challenge is complete, the collaborator access remains until the workshop ends -- you can keep helping each other as you work through the rest of Day 1.

#### Visibility

## The Learning Automation System

When you open a PR in the Learning Room, you get **three types of feedback**:

### Type 1: Automated Bot Feedback (30 seconds)

- Technical validation (links, headings, file locations)
- Accessibility checking (detailed)
- Educational messaging (WHY each thing matters)
- Links to learning resources
- Never fails the PR; always educational

### Type 2: Peer Reviewer Feedback (15-60 minutes)

- Human judgment on content
- Creative suggestions
- Encouragement and mentorship
- Understanding of context
- Can approve, request changes, or comment

### Type 3: Progress Tracking (on merge)

- Skill badges (Markdown Master, Accessibility Advocate)
- Level progression (Beginner → Intermediate → Advanced → Expert)
- Milestone celebrations (1st, 5th, 10th PR)
- Motivational comments

**Together:** Instant technical feedback + human mentorship + visible progress

## FAQ: Pull Requests in Your Learning Room

### "Can I see other students' PRs?"

Not inside their Learning Room repos -- those are private to each student. **You can see other participants' work in two ways:**

- During Challenge 3 ("Join the Conversation") and Challenge 8 ("Culture"), the facilitators pair you with classmates and add you as a collaborator on each other's repos so you can review.
- During Day 2 (and the Bonus C challenge), everyone contributes to the public `accessibility-agents` repo, where every PR is visible to everyone.

### "What if I don't agree with my assigned reviewer?"

When the facilitators pair you for peer review, the pairing is a starting point, not a mandate. You can request additional reviewers manually. Click "Reviewers" -> select someone else, or ask the facilitators to pair you differently.

### "Will my PR get lost when everyone is working at once?"

No. Your repo is your own; you only see your own PRs. Gandalf's feedback is on your PR alone, and any peer reviewer is specifically assigned to you.

### "Can I comment on someone else's PR?"

When the facilitators pair you for review, yes -- you will be added as a collaborator and can comment, approve, and request changes on their PR. On the public `accessibility-agents` repo, anyone can comment on any open PR.

### "What if my reviewer doesn't respond?"

Mention them directly in a PR comment: "@name, any thoughts on the changes I pushed?" Or ask a facilitator to follow up.

### "Can I work with a friend?"

The facilitators arrange peer pairings, but if you know someone else in the cohort and you want to review each other's work, ask either Jeff or Michael to add you to each other's repos.

### "How long does review take?"

When pairings happen during a workshop block, typically 15-60 minutes. If a reviewer is slow, the facilitators can step in or assign someone else.

### "What if bot feedback is wrong?"

Comment on the PR explaining why. Gandalf is intentionally educational, not punitive -- if you disagree with a check, the facilitators can override it. Gandalf is not perfect, which is exactly why human review still matters.

### "Do I need to complete every challenge?"

No. The Learning Room has challenges for all skill levels. You can pick what interests you, complete at your pace, and continue after the workshop -- your repo stays yours.

## If You Get Stuck

| Problem | What to do |
|---|---|
| Cannot find your `learn/<username>` branch | If you have not created it yet, follow Challenge 4. If you created it but cannot see it, refresh the branch selector or run `git fetch origin` from a local clone. |
| Push rejected to main branch | Main is protected. You need to push to your `learn/<username>` branch: `git checkout learn/<your-username>` then push again. |
| I want to see another student's PR | Ask a facilitator -- when peer review is part of a challenge, they will add you as a collaborator on the other student's repo. |
| Practice file has no TODO markers | Verify you are on the correct branch. Run `git branch` to see your current branch. The main branch may have already been updated. |
| Accidentally committed to main | Do not panic. See the failsafe instructions in [Chapter 13](13-how-git-works.md#10-if-you-get-stuck) or ask a facilitator. |
| Everything else | Post a comment on your challenge issue describing what happened. That always counts as participation. |
| I finished Challenge 4 but I am not sure I did it right | Compare your work against the [Challenge 4 reference solution](solutions/solution-04-branch-out.md). Any branch with any name is a success. |
| I finished Challenge 5 but I am not sure I did it right | Compare your work against the [Challenge 5 reference solution](solutions/solution-05-make-your-mark.md). Any clear edit with a descriptive commit message is a success. |
